analysis.one_liner: Bars states from taxing or regulating businesses that have no physical presence there.
analysis.headline: Backed by 12 House members including the Judiciary chairman, the bill was sent to committee in June 2017 and never received a vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop states from taxing, or requiring sales tax collection from, any business that is not physically present in the state — a standard that most online-only sellers meet. It would also stop states from imposing their own product rules on goods manufactured elsewhere. Companies could go to federal court to strike down state taxes or regulations that violated the bill. It never advanced past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Large online retailers, marketplace platforms, catalog companies, and other interstate sellers that ship into states where they own no stores, warehouses, or offices. They would be freed from collecting the sales tax that their customers owe and from complying with state-level product standards that go beyond federal rules. Platform middlemen, delivery carriers, and payment processors are explicitly written out of the definition of a 'seller,' so the tax duty would not reach them either.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits states from taxing a business — or making it collect sales tax — unless the business is physically present in the state during the period of the tax.

Defines physical presence narrowly: a commercial domicile, real property, on-site service workers, exclusive agents, or three or more regular employees in the state, so selling online into a state from elsewhere would not count.

Excludes marketplace providers, referral services, delivery carriers, and payment processors from the definition of a seller, so the collection obligation would not attach to the platforms that actually process most online purchases.

Prohibits states from imposing their own product standards on goods manufactured in other states unless federal law already requires them, sweeping in state rules on production, manufacturing, and disposal.
Gives federal district courts original jurisdiction, letting businesses sue to block state taxes or regulations they claim the act forbids, including immediate court orders.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, which would lose sales tax revenue their residents owe but rarely pay on remote purchases — money that funds schools, roads, and public services. Local stores would keep competing against online rivals who hold a tax advantage, and residents would lose state consumer and safety rules the federal government has not enacted.

drawbacks.text: States would lose sales tax owed by their own residents on remote purchases; residents legally owe 'use tax' on out-of-state buys but pay it at very low rates, so state budgets would absorb the loss and services or other taxes would make it up.

The definition of 'regulate' is broad enough to reach state product, safety, and labeling rules on goods made in other states, so state consumer protections stricter than federal law could be voided and challenged in federal court.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the counterargument: businesses selling nationwide face thousands of state and local tax jurisdictions, and the Supreme Court's 1992 physical-presence rule (Quill) existed partly because of that compliance burden. The bill went further than fixing that problem, however, by also wiping out state regulatory authority, not just tax collection duties.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core benefit goes to interstate sellers, who would keep a built-in price advantage over local stores and escape state rules, while the cost lands on state budgets and on residents who lose state protections with no federal replacement. The compliance-burden argument behind it is real but narrow; this bill used it to reach far beyond tax collection into state regulatory power generally.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2017, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then sent to a subcommittee a month later, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 — and the Supreme Court's 2018 Wayfair decision letting states tax remote sales made the tax half of it moot anyway.

narrative.text: Representative Sensenbrenner introduced the bill on June 12, 2017, joined by seven original cosponsors, all Republicans.
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced.
On July 19, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law, where action ended.
The bill finished with 11 cosponsors, 10 Republicans and 1 Democrat, and no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments and local retailers came out ahead: the bill never became law, so states kept their taxing and regulatory authority over interstate sellers, and the Supreme Court's 2018 Wayfair ruling independently cleared the way for states to require remote sellers to collect sales tax.

for.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as an original cosponsor; the committee he chaired never acted on it.

for.name: Amazon
for.what_they_did: Publicly endorsed the bill, which exempts marketplace platforms from sales tax collection duties.

for.name: eBay
for.what_they_did: Publicly supported the bill, which shields its sellers from state tax collection requirements.

against.name: National Governors Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing it would strip states of sales tax revenue and regulatory authority owed to their residents.

against.name: National Conference of State Legislatures
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against federal physical-presence mandates like this bill, which would override state tax law.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split 10 Republicans to 1 Democrat; the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll call to break down.

industries.note: The bill would let online-only sellers ship into states without collecting the sales tax their customers owe, and the platform role (Amazon-style marketplaces) is explicitly excluded from any tax duty. Their gain comes at the direct expense of state revenues and of local stores competing on uneven terms.

States would lose sales tax their residents owe but rarely pay voluntarily, and would lose the power to set product and safety rules stricter than federal law. Their loss is the public's loss of revenue and consumer protections.
Online rivals would keep a built-in price advantage from uncollected sales tax, entrenching an uneven playing field against local stores.
Mail-order and remote sellers would escape tax collection obligations in nearly every state where they lack a warehouse or office, preserving their historical price advantage.
